🛍️ Customer Segmentation Engine — Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Dataset: UK Online Retail — Kaggle: carrie1/ecommerce-data (541k transactions, Dec 2010 – Dec 2011)

Target: None — this is an unsupervised problem. There is no label to predict; the goal is to discover natural customer groupings from behavioural data.

Author: Data Science Team

🏬 Business Problem¶

A retail/e-commerce business (and the consulting teams that advise it — think Myntra, HDFC Bank, McKinsey) sends the same generic marketing email, the same discount code, and the same product recommendations to every customer. This is expensive and ineffective: a customer who orders every week and a customer who bought once eight months ago do not respond to the same offer.

Goal: Group ~4,000 customers into a small number of behaviourally distinct segments using RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis combined with K-Means and DBSCAN clustering, so that:

  • Marketing spend can be targeted per-segment (e.g. win-back offers for lapsing customers, loyalty perks for champions) instead of blanket campaigns.
  • High-value "VIP" customers can be identified and protected from churn before they disengage.
  • Low-value / one-time customers can be nurtured cheaply (email only) instead of receiving costly discount codes.
  • The resulting segments feed directly into a production customer_segmentation_pipeline.py that scores new/returning customers weekly.

This notebook follows the same EDA discipline as the Credit Risk and Fraud Detection notebooks in this project: every plot has a Why, every plot yields an Observation, and every observation drives a concrete Pipeline/Engineering decision.

Step 1 — Import Libraries¶

Why: All required libraries are imported upfront. sklearn.cluster provides both KMeans (centroid-based, needs a pre-specified k) and DBSCAN (density-based, discovers k automatically and flags outliers as noise) so the two paradigms can be compared directly. NearestNeighbors is used later to build the k-distance plot that drives DBSCAN's eps parameter.

In [2]:

Step 2 — Data Loading and Initial Inspection¶

Why: First look at the raw transaction log — shape, column names, and a transposed head() for easy reading. Unlike the credit risk / fraud notebooks, this dataset is transaction-level, not customer-level — each row is one product line on one invoice, so the same customer appears in hundreds of rows. Customer-level features (RFM) must be engineered before clustering — that is the core job of this notebook.

Business context: DATA_PATH points to the raw Kaggle CSV (Online Retail.csv / data.csv) as downloaded locally. If that file is not present — as in this sandboxed run — a schema-faithful synthetic reconstruction (same 8 columns, same missingness pattern, same order-of-magnitude row count, fixed seed for reproducibility) is generated instead, so the notebook logic below is identical whether it runs on the real Kaggle file or this fallback. Swapping in the real CSV requires no code changes.

In [3]:
import os

DATA_PATH = r"D:\Data Science Datasets\Customer Segmentation Engine\data.csv"


def generate_synthetic_online_retail(n_customers=4000, seed=42):
    '''Schema-faithful synthetic reconstruction of the UK Online Retail dataset.
    Bakes in 6 latent customer personas (champion/loyal/new/at_risk/hibernating/regular)
    so downstream RFM clusters are realistically separable, exactly as in real retail data.
    '''
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    start, end = pd.Timestamp('2010-12-01'), pd.Timestamp('2011-12-09')
    snapshot = end + pd.Timedelta(days=1)

    personas = rng.choice(['champion', 'loyal', 'new', 'at_risk', 'hibernating', 'regular'],
                           size=n_customers, p=[0.05, 0.15, 0.15, 0.15, 0.25, 0.25])
    persona_cfg = {
        'champion':    dict(n_orders=(20, 45), recency_days=(0, 20)),
        'loyal':       dict(n_orders=(10, 22), recency_days=(0, 45)),
        'new':         dict(n_orders=(1, 3),   recency_days=(0, 30)),
        'at_risk':     dict(n_orders=(6, 15),  recency_days=(120, 250)),
        'hibernating': dict(n_orders=(1, 4),   recency_days=(180, 340)),
        'regular':     dict(n_orders=(3, 9),   recency_days=(20, 160)),
    }
    customer_ids = np.arange(12346, 12346 + n_customers)
    country_pool = (['United Kingdom'] * 88 + ['Germany'] * 3 + ['France'] * 3 + ['EIRE'] * 2 +
                     ['Netherlands'] * 1 + ['Spain'] * 1 + ['Belgium'] * 1 + ['Switzerland'] * 1)
    customer_country = rng.choice(country_pool, size=n_customers)

    products = [f'P{str(i).zfill(4)}' for i in range(1, 251)]
    descriptions = {p: f'GIFT ITEM {i}' for i, p in enumerate(products, start=1)}
    unit_price_base = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=1.8, size=250) + 0.39

    rows, invoice_counter = [], 536365
    for idx, cust in enumerate(customer_ids):
        cfg = persona_cfg[personas[idx]]
        n_orders = rng.integers(cfg['n_orders'][0], cfg['n_orders'][1] + 1)
        last_gap = rng.integers(cfg['recency_days'][0], cfg['recency_days'][1] + 1)
        last_order_date = snapshot - pd.Timedelta(days=int(last_gap))
        if n_orders > 1:
            gaps = np.sort(rng.integers(1, 300, size=n_orders - 1))
            order_dates = [last_order_date] + [last_order_date - pd.Timedelta(days=int(g)) for g in gaps]
        else:
            order_dates = [last_order_date]
        for od in order_dates:
            od = max(od, start)
            invoice_counter += 1
            invoice_no = str(invoice_counter)
            is_cancel = rng.random() < 0.02
            n_lines = rng.integers(1, 12)
            line_products = rng.choice(products, size=n_lines, replace=False)
            for p in line_products:
                price = round(max(0.35, unit_price_base[products.index(p)] * rng.normal(1.0, 0.08)), 2)
                qty = rng.integers(1, 12)
                if rng.random() < 0.03:
                    qty = rng.integers(20, 200)  # occasional wholesale-style bulk line
                invoice_out = ('C' + invoice_no) if is_cancel else invoice_no
                qty = -abs(qty) if is_cancel else qty
                rows.append((invoice_out, p, descriptions[p], qty, od, price, cust, customer_country[idx]))

    data = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['InvoiceNo', 'StockCode', 'Description', 'Quantity',
                                        'InvoiceDate', 'UnitPrice', 'CustomerID', 'Country'])
    # ~28% guest checkouts -> missing CustomerID, matching real dataset's ~25% missingness
    guest = data.sample(n=int(len(data) * 0.28), random_state=1).copy()
    guest['CustomerID'] = np.nan
    data = pd.concat([data, guest], ignore_index=True)
    err_idx = rng.choice(data.index, size=int(len(data) * 0.004), replace=False)
    data.loc[err_idx, 'UnitPrice'] = 0.0
    desc_idx = rng.choice(data.index, size=int(len(data) * 0.002), replace=False)
    data.loc[desc_idx, 'Description'] = np.nan
    data = pd.concat([data, data.sample(n=57, random_state=3)], ignore_index=True)  # inject exact dupes
    return data.sample(frac=1.0, random_state=7).reset_index(drop=True)


if os.path.exists(DATA_PATH):
    df_raw = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, encoding='ISO-8859-1')
    print('✅ Loaded real Kaggle UK Online Retail dataset from DATA_PATH')
else:
    df_raw = generate_synthetic_online_retail(n_customers=4000, seed=RANDOM_STATE)
    print('⚠ DATA_PATH not found — using schema-faithful synthetic reconstruction (seed=42) for this run')

print(f'Columns      : {list(df_raw.columns)}')

Step 3 — Dataset Structure and Data Types¶

Why: Understanding dtypes before any transformation matters here specifically because InvoiceDate typically loads as a string/object, not a datetime — every downstream Recency calculation depends on it being parsed correctly. InvoiceNo and StockCode also need to stay as strings, since some invoice numbers carry a leading 'C' (cancellations) and some stock codes are alphanumeric (e.g. postage, manual adjustments).

💡 Pipeline decision: Date parsing is fixed as a mandatory first transform in validate_input_data() — every RFM feature below depends on InvoiceDate being a true datetime, not a string.

Step 4 — Missing Values Analysis¶

Why: Missing values must be identified before any aggregation. Unlike the credit risk / fraud datasets, this dataset is expected to have missingness — CustomerID is often blank for guest checkouts, and a small fraction of Description fields are blank due to manual stock adjustments. Visualizing with a heatmap makes the pattern of missingness (structural vs. random) obvious in a way row counts cannot.

Business insight: A missing CustomerID is not noise — it means "we cannot attribute this revenue to a person," which directly determines whether a transaction can even participate in segmentation.

In [5]:

📌 Observation: CustomerID is missing in 24.9% of all line items (135,080 of 541,909 rows) — these are guest/unauthenticated checkouts. Description is missing in a much smaller 0.27% of rows (1,454 rows), consistent with manual stock-adjustment entries that carry no product text. Quantity, UnitPrice, InvoiceNo, StockCode, InvoiceDate, and Country are fully populated.

💡 Pipeline decision: Rows with missing CustomerID are dropped only from the segmentation table, not from the raw log — they still count toward overall revenue/AOV reporting elsewhere, but a customer cannot be clustered without an identity to attach the cluster label to. Missing Description is left as-is; it does not affect RFM math.

Step 5 — Duplicate Detection and Data Cleaning¶

Why: Exact duplicate rows (same invoice, product, quantity, price, customer, timestamp) are almost always double-scanned line items or export artifacts, not genuine repeat purchases. Left in place, they silently inflate a customer's Frequency and Monetary values — directly biasing the clustering input.

In [6]:
dupes = df_raw.duplicated().sum()
print(f'Duplicate rows found : {dupes} ({dupes/len(df_raw)*100:.2f}% of rows)')

df = df_raw.drop_duplicates(ignore_index=True)
print(f'Shape before cleaning : {df_raw.shape}')
print(f'Shape after  cleaning : {df.shape}')
print(f'Rows removed          : {df_raw.shape[0] - df.shape[0]}')

Duplicate rows found : 5268 (0.97% of rows)
Shape before cleaning : (541909, 8)
Shape after  cleaning : (536641, 8)
Rows removed          : 5268

📌 Observation: 5,268 exact duplicate rows (0.97% of the raw data) are present and removed. This is a routine but necessary step — even a modest number of duplicated high-value orders can shift a customer's Frequency/Monetary enough to move them into a different cluster.

💡 Pipeline decision: drop_duplicates() runs immediately after load, before any aggregation, and is baked into validate_input_data() so every future weekly batch is deduplicated identically before RFM is recomputed.

Step 6 — Data Quality Issues: Cancellations and Invalid Transactions¶

Why: Retail transaction logs contain three known contaminants that don't exist in the credit-risk/fraud datasets: cancellations (InvoiceNo prefixed with 'C', Quantity negative — a refund, not a purchase), non-positive quantities/prices (returns, samples, manual write-offs), and non-product stock codes (postage, bank charges, manual adjustments). All three must be quantified before deciding what counts as a "real purchase" for RFM.

Business insight: A customer who orders heavily and then cancels everything is not a loyal customer — including their cancelled lines in Monetary would wrongly flag them as high-value.

In [7]:
df['IsCancelled'] = df['InvoiceNo'].astype(str).str.startswith('C')
neg_qty = (df['Quantity'] <= 0) & (~df['IsCancelled'])
non_positive_price = df['UnitPrice'] <= 0

for bar, v in zip(bars, counts):

Cancellation rate         : 1.72%
Non-positive price rows   : 2,512 (0.47%)

📌 Observation: 1.72% of invoices are cancellations, cleanly identifiable by the 'C' prefix and negative quantity. The monthly cancellation rate fluctuates between roughly 1.3% and 2.0% with no single bad period driving it — it dips notably in the final (partial) month. Two additional quality issues surface here that a synthetic dataset wouldn't show: 1,336 rows (0.25%) have non-positive Quantity on a non-cancelled invoice (likely manual stock corrections), and 2,512 rows (0.47%) have non-positive UnitPrice (goodwill items / write-offs / data entry at zero cost).

💡 Pipeline decision: df_clean is defined as: not cancelled AND Quantity > 0 AND UnitPrice > 0 AND CustomerID not null — this single filter also absorbs the two extra issues found above (non-cancelled negative-quantity rows and zero-price rows), since both fail the Quantity > 0 / UnitPrice > 0 conditions without needing a separate rule. Cancellations are logged separately as a RefundRate feature per customer for a later churn-risk extension, but excluded from Monetary.

Step 7 — Statistical Summary Heatmap (Quantity & UnitPrice)¶

Why: Before building df_clean, it's worth profiling the raw economics of Quantity and UnitPrice across their full range (including the values about to be filtered out) — a normalized heatmap makes it immediately obvious which statistic (mean, max, std) is being pulled by extreme values.

In [8]:
desc = df[['Quantity', 'UnitPrice']].describe().T
desc['cv'] = (desc['std'] / desc['mean'].abs()).round(3)
desc['range'] = (desc['max'] - desc['min']).round(2)
display(desc.round(2))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))
sns.heatmap(heat_data, annot=desc[cols_to_plot].round(1), fmt='g', cmap='YlOrRd', linewidths=0.5, linecolor='white')
plt.title('Normalized Statistical Summary — Quantity & UnitPrice\nDarker = higher relative value', fontweight='bold')

count mean std min 25% 50% 75% max cv range
Quantity 536641.0 9.62 219.13 -80995.00 1.00 3.00 10.00 80995.0 22.78 161990.00
UnitPrice 536641.0 4.63 97.23 -11062.06 1.25 2.08 4.13 38970.0 20.99 50032.06

📌 Observation: The real data reveals a specific, extreme data-quality artifact that the earlier synthetic run did not surface: Quantity ranges from -80,995 to +80,995 — a single matched pair (one enormous bulk order, later fully cancelled), and UnitPrice ranges from -11,062.06 (a large negative "bad debt adjustment" entry) to 38,970 (an anomalous manual/fee entry, not a real per-unit product price). Both features show a coefficient of variation over 20x their mean, confirming these are not just "a bit skewed" but dominated by a handful of extreme, mechanically distinct entries.

💡 Pipeline decision: This confirms the Step 6 filtering strategy is not optional but necessary: cap/clip must happen after removing cancellations and non-positive prices, never before — the ±80,995 pair and the -11,062.06 adjustment are exactly the kind of non-product entries that filtering (not clipping) needs to remove outright, since they are data artifacts rather than genuine bulk-purchase signal.

Step 8 — Outlier Detection: Quantity and UnitPrice (Post-Cleaning)¶

Why: Now that cancellations and invalid rows are excluded, remaining extreme values in Quantity and UnitPrice are genuine — they typically represent wholesale/bulk buyers rather than errors. Boxplots on a log scale make both the typical range and the tail visible in one view, which a linear-scale boxplot cannot do here given how heavy the tail is.

In [9]:
df_clean_preview = df[(~df['IsCancelled']) & (df['Quantity'] > 0) & (df['UnitPrice'] > 0) & (df['CustomerID'].notna())].copy()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, col, color in zip(axes, ['Quantity', 'UnitPrice'], [BLUE, PINK]):
    ax.boxplot(df_clean_preview[col], patch_artist=True, vert=True,
               boxprops=dict(facecolor=color, alpha=0.6), medianprops=dict(color='white', linewidth=2.5),
               flierprops=dict(marker='o', markerfacecolor=GRAY, markersize=3, alpha=0.3))
    ax.set_yscale('log')
    ax.set_title(f'{col} (log scale)\nskew={df_clean_preview[col].skew():.2f}')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

q1, q3 = df_clean_preview['Quantity'].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
n_outliers = ((df_clean_preview['Quantity'] < q1 - 1.5*iqr) | (df_clean_preview['Quantity'] > q3 + 1.5*iqr)).sum()
print(f"Quantity IQR outliers : {n_outliers:,} rows ({n_outliers/len(df_clean_preview)*100:.2f}%)")

Quantity IQR outliers : 25,616 rows (6.52%)

📌 Observation: Even after cleaning, Quantity and UnitPrice remain extremely right-skewed — skewness of 407 and 203 respectively, far beyond what log-scaling alone can visually normalize (the log-scale boxplots still show dense outlier clouds above the whisker). IQR flags 25,616 rows (6.52%) of the cleaned data as Quantity outliers. This is a much heavier tail than typical retail data, consistent with a customer base that mixes ordinary retail buyers with a small number of small-business/wholesale accounts.

💡 Pipeline decision: Line-item-level outliers are still not clipped at this stage — with skew this extreme, clipping raw transaction rows would risk deleting genuine wholesale signal alongside noise. The decision is deferred to the aggregated customer-level RFM table (Step 16), where IQR capping can be applied with full visibility into whether a "big number" belongs to a real repeat wholesale customer or a one-off artifact.

Step 9 — Transaction Volume Over Time¶

Why: RFM's "Recency" feature is only meaningful relative to a fixed snapshot date, and that snapshot must be chosen with the underlying seasonality in mind — if the data cuts off right after a seasonal peak (e.g. a holiday rush), every recent buyer will look artificially "Recent" regardless of their true underlying loyalty.

In [10]:
df_clean_preview['LineRevenue'] = df_clean_preview['Quantity'] * df_clean_preview['UnitPrice']
monthly = df_clean_preview.set_index('InvoiceDate').resample('ME').agg(
    Orders=('InvoiceNo', 'nunique'), Revenue=('LineRevenue', 'sum')
)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(monthly.index, monthly['Orders'], marker='o', color=BLUE)
axes[0].set_title('Distinct Orders per Month'); axes[0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
axes[1].bar(monthly.index, monthly['Revenue'], width=20, color=GREEN)
axes[1].set_title('Gross Revenue per Month'); axes[1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"Observation window : {df_clean_preview['InvoiceDate'].min().date()} → {df_clean_preview['InvoiceDate'].max().date()}")

Observation window : 2010-12-01 → 2011-12-09

📌 Observation: Both order volume and revenue climb steadily from a spring low, then roughly double between September and November 2011 — a clear pre-holiday sales ramp. The sharp drop visible in the final bar (Dec 2011) is not a real decline — it's a partial-month artifact, since data collection stops on 2011-12-09 rather than at month-end.

💡 Pipeline decision: The RFM snapshot date is fixed at one day after the last transaction in the data (2011-12-10, i.e. max(InvoiceDate) + 1 day), the standard convention — this keeps Recency comparable across all customers. The partial final month is also a flag for production: any monthly reporting job must treat the most recent month as provisional until it closes, or it will visually understate recent performance.

Step 10 — Country-wise Distribution of Transactions¶

Why: Country is a natural candidate confound: if 85%+ of revenue comes from one country, segmenting within that country vs. across all countries could produce different personas. It also flags whether a Country feature is worth adding to the clustering input at all.

In [11]:
country_rev = df_clean_preview.assign(Revenue=df_clean_preview['Quantity']*df_clean_preview['UnitPrice']) \
                               .groupby('Country')['Revenue'].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
top10 = country_rev.head(10)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
bars = ax.barh(top10.index[::-1], top10.values[::-1], color=BLUE, edgecolor='white')
ax.set_title('Top 10 Countries by Revenue'); ax.set_xlabel('Revenue')
for bar, v in zip(bars, top10.values[::-1]):
    ax.text(bar.get_width(), bar.get_y()+bar.get_height()/2, f' {v:,.0f} ({v/country_rev.sum()*100:.1f}%)', va='center', fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: The United Kingdom accounts for 82.0% of total revenue. The next-largest markets are all small by comparison: Netherlands (3.2%), EIRE (3.0%), Germany (2.6%), France (2.4%), and Australia (1.6%) — the remaining ~7% is spread across a long tail of smaller countries.

💡 Pipeline decision: Country is excluded from the clustering feature set — with one country holding over four-fifths of revenue, it would not meaningfully separate customers and would only add noise/dimensionality. It is retained as a reporting cut (Step 26) so segments can still be sliced by country for regional campaign targeting.

Step 11 — Building the Clean Transaction Table (df_clean)¶

Why: This is the formal checkpoint where every finding from Steps 4–8 is applied at once to produce the single clean, line-item-level table that all customer-level aggregation (Step 12 onward) will read from. Keeping this as one explicit, auditable step — rather than scattering filters throughout — is what makes the pipeline reproducible.

Business insight: TotalPrice = Quantity × UnitPrice is the revenue contribution of a single product line — the atomic unit that Monetary is built from.

In [12]:
df_clean = df[
    (~df['IsCancelled']) &
    (df['Quantity'] > 0) &
    (df['UnitPrice'] > 0) &
    (df['CustomerID'].notna())
].copy()

df_clean['CustomerID'] = df_clean['CustomerID'].astype(int)
df_clean['TotalPrice'] = df_clean['Quantity'] * df_clean['UnitPrice']

print(f'Raw rows              : {len(df_raw):,}')
print(f'After dedup           : {len(df):,}')
print(f'After quality filters : {len(df_clean):,}  ({len(df_clean)/len(df_raw)*100:.1f}% retained)')
print(f"Unique customers       : {df_clean['CustomerID'].nunique():,}")
print(f"Total revenue in scope : {df_clean['TotalPrice'].sum():,.0f}")

Raw rows              : 541,909
After dedup           : 536,641
After quality filters : 392,692  (72.5% retained)
Unique customers       : 4,338
Total revenue in scope : 8,887,209

📌 Observation: After all quality filters, 72.5% of raw rows are retained (392,692 of 541,909), covering 4,338 unique customers and £8,887,209 of in-scope revenue. The 27.5% excluded is the combined effect of missing CustomerID (24.9%), cancellations (1.72%), and non-positive quantity/price rows — with some overlap between these categories.

💡 Pipeline decision: df_clean is the single frozen input to feature engineering from this point forward. This exact filter chain is packaged as clean_transactions(df_raw) in the production pipeline, so training and inference apply identical logic.

Step 12 — RFM Feature Engineering (Recency, Frequency, Monetary)¶

Why: RFM is the industry-standard feature set for customer segmentation precisely because all three dimensions are behavioural, not demographic — they require no survey data, just transaction history, and each answers a distinct business question:

  • Recency — days since last purchase (lower = more engaged)
  • Frequency — number of distinct invoices (higher = more loyal)
  • Monetary — total revenue contributed (higher = more valuable)

Business insight: This is the single most important transformation in the notebook — it converts a 190k-row transaction log into a ~4,000-row customer-level table, which is the actual unit of analysis for clustering.

In [13]:
snapshot_date = df_clean['InvoiceDate'].max() + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
print(f'Snapshot date : {snapshot_date.date()}  (max InvoiceDate + 1 day)')

rfm = df_clean.groupby('CustomerID').agg(
    Recency=('InvoiceDate', lambda x: (snapshot_date - x.max()).days),
    Frequency=('InvoiceNo', 'nunique'),
    Monetary=('TotalPrice', 'sum'),
).reset_index()

print(f'\nCustomer-level RFM table : {rfm.shape}')
display(rfm.describe().round(2))
rfm.head()

📌 Observation: The RFM table confirms a genuine mix of active and lapsed customers. Notably, customer 12346 — the very first row — has Recency=326, Frequency=1, Monetary=77,183.60: a single enormous order and nothing since. This is the same customer behind the ±80,995-unit cancelled/reordered pair flagged in Step 7 — a real example of why a customer-level view is essential: a transaction-level scan would show this as noise, but at the customer level it's clearly one extreme, one-time account. Frequency's mean is well above its median, and Monetary's max is more than an order of magnitude above its median — both classic right-skew signatures that will need addressing before distance-based clustering.

💡 Pipeline decision: rfm becomes the base table for every subsequent step. snapshot_date is stored as a pipeline constant (2011-12-10, i.e. max(InvoiceDate)+1) recomputed on each production run. Extreme single-order customers like 12346 are not removed — they are handled downstream via IQR capping (Step 16), since deleting them would silently discard the business's actual highest-spending account.

Step 13 — RFM Distribution Analysis (Univariate)¶

Why: Distribution shape determines the preprocessing each feature needs before clustering. K-Means and DBSCAN are both distance-based — a heavily right-skewed feature like Monetary will dominate the Euclidean distance calculation purely because of scale and long tail, drowning out Recency and Frequency regardless of their true business importance.

In [14]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 8))
for i, col in enumerate(['Recency', 'Frequency', 'Monetary']):
    skew = rfm[col].skew()
    color = PINK if abs(skew) > 1 else BLUE
    sns.histplot(rfm[col], kde=True, bins=40, color=color, edgecolor='white', ax=axes[0, i])
    axes[0, i].set_title(f'{col}\nskewness={skew:.2f}', fontweight='bold')
    label = 'RIGHT SKEWED ⚠' if skew > 1 else 'APPROX NORMAL ✅'
    axes[0, i].text(0.97, 0.95, label, transform=axes[0, i].transAxes, ha='right', va='top',
                     fontsize=9, color=PINK if '⚠' in label else GREEN, fontweight='bold')
    axes[1, i].boxplot(rfm[col], patch_artist=True, boxprops=dict(facecolor=color, alpha=0.6),
                        medianprops=dict(color='white', linewidth=2.5),
                        flierprops=dict(marker='o', markerfacecolor=GRAY, markersize=3, alpha=0.4))
    axes[1, i].set_xticklabels([col])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: All three RFM features are flagged right-skewed, but by very different margins. Frequency (skew=12.07) and Monetary (skew=19.34) are extremely skewed — long tails of high-value/high-frequency customers. Recency (skew=1.25) is also technically right-skewed (more early/recent activity, thinning out toward the full window), but nowhere near as extreme — an order of magnitude milder than the other two.

💡 Pipeline decision: Frequency and Monetary are flagged for log1p transformation before scaling (Step 15) — mandatory given skew in the double digits. Recency is left on its natural scale: its mild skew (1.25) does not distort Euclidean distance nearly as severely, it stays directly interpretable in days for business reporting, and log-transforming it would add complexity for little practical gain.

Step 14 — RFM Correlation Analysis¶

Why: If two of the three RFM dimensions are highly correlated, clustering on all three effectively double-counts one underlying signal, distorting cluster shapes. Frequency and Monetary are commonly correlated (customers who order often also tend to spend more in total) — the question is how strongly, and whether it's strong enough to warrant dropping a dimension.

In [15]:
corr = rfm[['Recency', 'Frequency', 'Monetary']].corr()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, ax=axes[0], linewidths=0.5)
axes[0].set_title('RFM Correlation Matrix')

axes[1].scatter(rfm['Frequency'], rfm['Monetary'], s=10, alpha=0.4, color=BLUE)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Frequency'); axes[1].set_ylabel('Monetary')
axes[1].set_title(f"Frequency vs Monetary (r={corr.loc['Frequency','Monetary']:.2f})")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: Frequency and Monetary correlate at r=0.55 — positive as expected, but with clear spread rather than near-collinearity (some low-frequency customers still post high Monetary via large basket size, and vice versa). Recency correlates weakly with both: r=-0.26 with Frequency and r=-0.12 with Monetary — lapsed customers skew slightly toward lower historical frequency/spend, but the relationship is far from deterministic.

💡 Pipeline decision: All three RFM dimensions are retained for clustering — none is dropped for redundancy. The moderate Frequency–Monetary correlation (0.55) is acceptable for K-Means/DBSCAN, which do not assume feature independence the way linear regression does.

Step 15 — Skewness Correction via Log Transformation¶

Why: Following the Step 13 finding, Frequency and Monetary are log1p-transformed (log(1+x), safe for zero values) to compress their long right tails before scaling. This directly determines how well-separated clusters will be — without this step, K-Means would essentially just re-discover "high spenders" as one axis and ignore Recency/Frequency nuance.

In [16]:
rfm_log = rfm.copy()
rfm_log['Frequency_log'] = np.log1p(rfm_log['Frequency'])
rfm_log['Monetary_log'] = np.log1p(rfm_log['Monetary'])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for ax, raw_col, log_col in zip(axes, ['Frequency', 'Monetary'], ['Frequency_log', 'Monetary_log']):
    sns.histplot(rfm_log[raw_col], color=GRAY, kde=True, ax=ax, label=f'raw (skew={rfm_log[raw_col].skew():.2f})', alpha=0.5)
    sns.histplot(rfm_log[log_col], color=GREEN, kde=True, ax=ax, label=f'log1p (skew={rfm_log[log_col].skew():.2f})', alpha=0.5)
    ax.set_title(raw_col); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: log1p transformation is highly effective here: Frequency's skewness drops from 12.07 to 1.21, and Monetary's drops from 19.34 to 0.40 — both now close to symmetric and far better suited to Euclidean-distance-based clustering.

💡 Pipeline decision: log1p(Frequency) and log1p(Monetary) replace the raw columns in the clustering feature set; Recency stays untransformed per the Step 13 decision. This exact transform is embedded in the RFMTransformer step of the production ColumnTransformer.

Step 16 — Outlier Treatment on the Customer-Level RFM Table¶

Why: Even after log transformation, a handful of extreme wholesale-style customers can pull K-Means centroids toward themselves, distorting the segment boundaries for the remaining "normal" retail customers. Per the Step 8 decision, capping happens here — on the aggregated customer table — not on raw transaction rows, preserving legitimate bulk-order signal while preventing a tiny handful of extreme accounts from single-handedly defining a cluster.

In [17]:
def iqr_cap(s, k=1.5):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return s.clip(q1 - k * iqr, q3 + k * iqr), (s < q1 - k*iqr).sum() + (s > q3 + k*iqr).sum()

rfm_capped = rfm_log.copy()
cap_report = {}
for col in ['Recency', 'Frequency_log', 'Monetary_log']:
    rfm_capped[col], n_capped = iqr_cap(rfm_capped[col])
    cap_report[col] = n_capped

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.5))
for ax, col in zip(axes, ['Recency', 'Frequency_log', 'Monetary_log']):
    ax.boxplot([rfm_log[col], rfm_capped[col]], patch_artist=True, labels=['before', 'after'],
               boxprops=dict(facecolor=BLUE, alpha=0.6), medianprops=dict(color='white', linewidth=2))
    ax.set_title(f'{col}\ncapped: {cap_report[col]} customers')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(cap_report)

{'Recency': 155, 'Frequency_log': 42, 'Monetary_log': 52}

📌 Observation: IQR capping affects a small, consistent share of customers per dimension: 155 customers (3.6%) on Recency, 42 (1.0%) on log-Frequency, and 52 (1.2%) on log-Monetary. Even the log-transformed features still carry enough tail to trigger capping for roughly 1% of the base — confirming these are genuine outliers, not a large distorted subgroup.

💡 Pipeline decision: IQRCapper(k=1.5) is fitted on the training RFM table only and applied identically at inference — capped customers are kept, not dropped, since even a capped "extreme value" (like customer 12346 from Step 12) retains its relative rank as one of the highest-value customers in the dataset.

Step 17 — Feature Scaling for Clustering¶

Why: K-Means and DBSCAN both compute Euclidean distance between points. Recency (range: days, up to hundreds) and log-Frequency (range: single digits) live on completely different numeric scales — without standardization, Recency alone would dominate every distance calculation regardless of its true importance.

In [18]:
feature_cols = ['Recency', 'Frequency_log', 'Monetary_log']
X = rfm_capped[feature_cols].copy()

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
X_scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(X_scaled, columns=feature_cols)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
X.boxplot(ax=axes[0]); axes[0].set_title('Before Scaling (raw units)')
X_scaled_df.boxplot(ax=axes[1]); axes[1].set_title('After StandardScaler (mean=0, std=1)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(pd.DataFrame(X_scaled, columns=feature_cols).describe().round(2).loc[['mean', 'std']])

      Recency  Frequency_log  Monetary_log
mean      0.0           -0.0          -0.0
std       1.0            1.0           1.0

📌 Observation: All three features now share a common mean-zero, unit-variance scale, and their relative spreads (interquartile ranges) are visually comparable for the first time — a prerequisite that was clearly violated before scaling.

💡 Pipeline decision: StandardScaler is fitted once on the full customer base and saved as scaler.pkl; production inference applies scaler.transform() (never fit_transform()) to new customer batches so cluster boundaries stay stable over time.

Step 18 — Optimal K: Elbow Method (WCSS)¶

Why: K-Means requires the number of clusters k to be chosen in advance. The elbow method plots within-cluster sum of squares (inertia) against k — inertia always decreases as k grows, but the rate of decrease slows sharply past the "true" number of natural groups, producing a visible bend.

In [19]:
wcss = []
K_range = range(2, 10)
for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_init=10).fit(X_scaled)
    wcss.append(km.inertia_)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(list(K_range), wcss, marker='o', color=BLUE, linewidth=2)
plt.axvline(4, color=PINK, linestyle='--', label='candidate elbow: k=4')
plt.xlabel('Number of clusters (k)'); plt.ylabel('WCSS (inertia)')
plt.title('Elbow Method for Optimal k'); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for k, w in zip(K_range, wcss):
    print(f'k={k}: WCSS={w:.1f}')

k=2: WCSS=6693.8
k=3: WCSS=4112.6
k=4: WCSS=3072.1
k=5: WCSS=2608.1
k=6: WCSS=2240.4
k=7: WCSS=2031.4
k=8: WCSS=1837.9
k=9: WCSS=1698.9

📌 Observation: WCSS drops sharply from 6,693.8 (k=2) to 3,072.1 (k=4), then flattens more gradually afterward (2,608.1 at k=5, 1,698.9 at k=9) — the classic elbow shape, with the bend visually sitting between k=3 and k=4.

💡 Pipeline decision: k=3 and k=4 are both carried forward as candidates, to be discriminated with silhouette score (Step 19) before either is finalized — the elbow method alone is suggestive, not definitive.

Step 19 — Optimal K: Silhouette Analysis¶

Why: The elbow method's "bend" can be subjective. Silhouette score gives a single number per k, quantifying how well-separated and internally cohesive the resulting clusters are (range -1 to 1; higher is better) — a more rigorous cross-check on the k=4 candidate from Step 18.

In [20]:
sil_scores = []
for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_init=10).fit(X_scaled)
    sil_scores.append(silhouette_score(X_scaled, km.labels_))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(list(K_range), sil_scores, marker='o', color=GREEN, linewidth=2)
best_k = list(K_range)[int(np.argmax(sil_scores))]
axes[0].axvline(best_k, color=PINK, linestyle='--', label=f'best k={best_k}')
axes[0].set_xlabel('k'); axes[0].set_ylabel('Silhouette score'); axes[0].set_title('Silhouette Score vs k'); axes[0].legend()

km_k4 = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_init=10).fit(X_scaled)
sample_sil = silhouette_samples(X_scaled, km_k4.labels_)
y_lower = 0
for i in range(4):
    vals = np.sort(sample_sil[km_k4.labels_ == i])
    axes[1].fill_betweenx(np.arange(y_lower, y_lower+len(vals)), 0, vals, color=CLUSTER_PALETTE[i], alpha=0.8)
    y_lower += len(vals)
axes[1].axvline(silhouette_score(X_scaled, km_k4.labels_), color='black', linestyle='--', label='avg score')
axes[1].set_title('Silhouette Plot (k=4)'); axes[1].set_xlabel('Silhouette coefficient'); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f'Silhouette scores by k : {dict(zip(K_range, np.round(sil_scores, 3)))}')
print(f'Best k by silhouette   : {best_k}')

Silhouette scores by k : {2: 0.411, 3: 0.42, 4: 0.382, 5: 0.349, 6: 0.342, 7: 0.331, 8: 0.303, 9: 0.299}
Best k by silhouette   : 3

📌 Observation: Silhouette score peaks at k=3 (0.420), with k=4 next at 0.382 — a real gap of 0.038 (roughly a 9% relative drop), not a negligible one. Score then declines more steadily: 0.349 at k=5, down to 0.299 at k=9. The per-cluster silhouette plot for k=4 shows all four clusters with mostly positive coefficients and no cluster collapsing to near-zero width, i.e. no degenerate cluster forced by the extra split — the drop from k=3 is a real but modest cohesion cost, not a sign that k=4 is statistically unsound.

💡 Pipeline decision: k=4 is finalized over the statistically-higher k=3 — an explicit statistics-vs-business trade-off, made with the real gap in view rather than assuming it away. The 0.038 silhouette cost buys a segmentation where "low-engagement" customers split into New/Potential and Hibernating — two personas needing opposite campaigns (onboarding nurture vs. low-cost win-back) that would otherwise be merged into one undifferentiated group at k=3. This trade-off, and the actual numbers behind it, are documented directly in train_kmeans.py so a future retrain doesn't silently revert to the higher-silhouette k=3 without the same business review.

Step 20 — K-Means Clustering (Final Fit, k=4)¶

Why: With k finalized, the production K-Means model is fit on the full scaled RFM table and cluster labels are attached back to every customer — this is the actual segmentation output the business will act on.

In [21]:
kmeans_final = KMeans(n_clusters=4, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_init=10)
rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster'] = kmeans_final.fit_predict(X_scaled)

cluster_sizes = rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster'].value_counts().sort_index()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
bars = ax.bar(cluster_sizes.index.astype(str), cluster_sizes.values, color=CLUSTER_PALETTE[:4], edgecolor='white')
for bar, v in zip(bars, cluster_sizes.values):
    ax.text(bar.get_x()+bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height(), f'{v}\n({v/len(rfm_capped)*100:.1f}%)', ha='center', va='bottom', fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title('K-Means Cluster Sizes (k=4)'); ax.set_xlabel('Cluster'); ax.set_ylabel('Customers')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"Final silhouette score : {silhouette_score(X_scaled, rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster']):.3f}")

Final silhouette score : 0.382

📌 Observation: Cluster sizes are 1,430 (33.0%), 650 (15.0%), 1,302 (30.0%), and 956 (22.0%) — reasonably balanced, with no cluster collapsing to a handful of points. The smallest cluster (15%) is, as expected from the Step 21 profiling, the high-value "Champions" group — high-value segments are naturally smaller than the general base in most real customer populations.

💡 Pipeline decision: KMeans_Cluster is now a permanent column on the customer table. The fitted kmeans_final object (centroids) is serialized so that new customers can be assigned to the nearest existing segment at inference time via .predict(), without recomputing cluster boundaries from scratch each time.

Step 21 — Cluster Profiling: RFM by Segment¶

Why: Cluster numbers (0, 1, 2, 3) mean nothing to a marketing team. This step translates each numeric cluster into its actual RFM behaviour profile — the necessary bridge between the statistical output and a business-usable persona.

In [22]:

profile['Customers'] = rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster'].value_counts().sort_index()

📌 Observation: The four clusters separate cleanly along business-relevant lines. Cluster 1 (Recency≈20.3, Frequency≈14.8, Monetary≈8,587.5): frequent, big-spending, recent buyers. Cluster 3 (Recency≈252.8, Frequency≈1.4, Monetary≈465.7): long-lapsed, low-value — the clear "Hibernating" group. Cluster 0 (Recency≈47.5, Frequency≈4.0, Monetary≈1,666.1): a moderate, previously-engaged group with slipping recency. Cluster 2 (Recency≈56.9, Frequency≈1.5, Monetary≈366.8): recent but with very little purchase history — likely newer customers still building a relationship with the business.

💡 Pipeline decision: These four numeric profiles are mapped to named business personas in Step 25 (Champions=Cluster 1, At Risk=Cluster 0, New/Potential=Cluster 2, Hibernating=Cluster 3) — this mapping table becomes the lookup used by the marketing-automation pipeline to select the offer template per customer.

Step 22 — 2D Cluster Visualization via PCA¶

Why: RFM is a 3-dimensional feature space — impossible to fully visualize on a single 2D scatter plot. PCA projects the scaled features onto their two directions of maximum variance, giving a defensible 2D approximation of cluster separation for stakeholder presentations, while explicitly reporting how much variance is retained.

In [23]:
pca = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
pcs = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
rfm_capped['PC1'], rfm_capped['PC2'] = pcs[:, 0], pcs[:, 1]

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6))
for c in sorted(rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster'].unique()):
    mask = rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster'] == c
    plt.scatter(rfm_capped.loc[mask, 'PC1'], rfm_capped.loc[mask, 'PC2'], s=18, alpha=0.6,
                color=CLUSTER_PALETTE[c], label=f'Cluster {c} (n={mask.sum()})')
centroids_pca = pca.transform(kmeans_final.cluster_centers_)
plt.scatter(centroids_pca[:, 0], centroids_pca[:, 1], marker='X', s=250, c='black', edgecolor='white', linewidth=1.5, label='Centroids')
plt.xlabel(f'PC1 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]*100:.1f}% variance)')
plt.ylabel(f'PC2 ({pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]*100:.1f}% variance)')
plt.title('K-Means Clusters in PCA Space'); plt.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f'Total variance explained by PC1+PC2 : {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()*100:.1f}%')

Total variance explained by PC1+PC2 : 93.7%

📌 Observation: PC1 alone captures 72.5% of variance and PC2 adds another 21.2%, for 93.7% total — an unusually high share for a 2-component PCA, meaning very little structure is lost in this visualization. The four K-Means clusters appear as clean, near-pie-slice regions radiating from the centroids with only minor edge overlap — strong visual confirmation that k=4 captures real, well-separated structure rather than an arbitrary split.

💡 Pipeline decision: The PCA projection is used only for visualization/stakeholder reporting — clustering itself is always performed on the full 3-D scaled RFM space (Step 20), never on the 2 PCA components. Given 93.7% variance is retained here, a PCA-based clustering shortcut would likely have given very similar results in this specific case — but the pipeline does not rely on that holding true for future data refreshes.

Step 23 — DBSCAN: k-Distance Plot for eps Selection¶

Why: Unlike K-Means, DBSCAN does not require k to be specified — instead it needs two density parameters, eps (neighbourhood radius) and min_samples. The standard way to choose eps is the k-distance plot: sort each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour and look for the "knee" where distances start increasing sharply — that knee is a natural density threshold.

In [24]:
min_samples = 10
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples).fit(X_scaled)
distances, _ = nn.kneighbors(X_scaled)
k_dist = np.sort(distances[:, -1])

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(k_dist, color=BLUE)
plt.axhline(0.4, color=PINK, linestyle='--', label='candidate eps = 0.4')
plt.xlabel(f'Points sorted by {min_samples}-NN distance'); plt.ylabel(f'{min_samples}-NN distance')
plt.title('k-Distance Plot for DBSCAN eps Selection'); plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: The k-distance curve stays low and flat for the bulk of customers before rising sharply near the tail — the "knee" sits at roughly eps ≈ 0.4, which becomes the density radius candidate for DBSCAN.

💡 Pipeline decision: eps=0.4, min_samples=10 are selected as the DBSCAN parameters — min_samples is set to roughly 2× the feature-space dimensionality (a common heuristic), which also guards against declaring very small, statistically fragile clusters.

Step 24 — DBSCAN Clustering & Comparison with K-Means¶

Why: K-Means forces every customer into a segment, even genuinely atypical ones — DBSCAN's ability to label points as noise (outliers that don't belong to any dense cluster) is a distinct advantage for finding customers who don't fit any clean behavioural pattern, useful for manual review rather than automated campaign targeting.

In [25]:
dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=0.4, min_samples=10)
rfm_capped['DBSCAN_Cluster'] = dbscan.fit_predict(X_scaled)

n_db_clusters = len(set(dbscan.labels_)) - (1 if -1 in dbscan.labels_ else 0)
n_noise = (dbscan.labels_ == -1).sum()
mask = dbscan.labels_ != -1
db_sil = silhouette_score(X_scaled[mask], dbscan.labels_[mask]) if n_db_clusters >= 2 else np.nan

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.5))
for c in sorted(rfm_capped['DBSCAN_Cluster'].unique()):
    mask_c = rfm_capped['DBSCAN_Cluster'] == c
    color = GRAY if c == -1 else CLUSTER_PALETTE[c % len(CLUSTER_PALETTE)]
    label = f'Noise (n={mask_c.sum()})' if c == -1 else f'Cluster {c} (n={mask_c.sum()})'
    axes[0].scatter(rfm_capped.loc[mask_c, 'PC1'], rfm_capped.loc[mask_c, 'PC2'], s=18, alpha=0.6 if c != -1 else 0.3, color=color, label=label)
axes[0].set_title(f'DBSCAN Result — {n_db_clusters} clusters + {n_noise} noise points'); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_xlabel('PC1'); axes[0].set_ylabel('PC2')

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    'Metric': ['# clusters found', 'Silhouette score', 'Handles outliers?', 'Requires k upfront?'],
    'K-Means': [4, f"{silhouette_score(X_scaled, rfm_capped['KMeans_Cluster']):.3f}", 'No — forces assignment', 'Yes'],
    'DBSCAN': [n_db_clusters, f'{db_sil:.3f}' if not np.isnan(db_sil) else 'n/a', f'Yes — {n_noise} flagged as noise', 'No'],
})
axes[1].axis('off')
tbl = axes[1].table(cellText=comparison.values, colLabels=comparison.columns, loc='center', cellLoc='center')
tbl.auto_set_font_size(False); tbl.set_fontsize(10); tbl.scale(1, 2.2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
display(comparison)
Metric K-Means DBSCAN
0 # clusters found 4 3
1 Silhouette score 0.382 0.181
2 Handles outliers? No — forces assignment Yes — 108 flagged as noise
3 Requires k upfront? Yes No

📌 Observation: DBSCAN finds 3 clusters — sized 1,937 / 1,475 / 818, a reasonably even split, not one dominant blob — plus 108 noise points (2.5% of customers) genuinely too sparse to belong to any dense region. Its silhouette score on the non-noise points is 0.181, markedly below K-Means's 0.382 — density-based clustering here merges several distinct RFM behaviours into fewer, coarser groups rather than reproducing the four business-relevant segments K-Means finds.

💡 Pipeline decision: K-Means (k=4) is selected as the primary production segmentation model — it gives every customer an actionable label, four business-relevant segments, and a meaningfully higher silhouette score (0.382 vs 0.181). DBSCAN's 108 noise-flagged customers are kept as a secondary "unusual behaviour" list — passed to the customer-success team for manual review rather than an automated campaign, since these are the RFM combinations no clean density-based pattern can explain.

Step 25 — Mapping Clusters to Business Personas¶

Why: This is the translation layer between data science output and business action. Each cluster is renamed based on its Step 21 RFM profile, using thresholds relative to the customer base's own median — not arbitrary fixed numbers — so the labelling remains valid even as the customer base grows.

In [26]:
med_r, med_f, med_m = rfm_capped['Recency'].median(), rfm_capped['Frequency'].median(), rfm_capped['Monetary'].median()

def label_persona(row):
    if row['Recency'] <= med_r and row['Frequency'] >= med_f and row['Monetary'] >= med_m:
        return 'Champions'
    if row['Recency'] > med_r and row['Frequency'] >= med_f:
        return 'At Risk'
    if row['Recency'] <= med_r and row['Frequency'] < med_f:
        return 'New / Potential Loyalist'
    return 'Hibernating'

rfm_capped['Persona'] = rfm_capped.apply(label_persona, axis=1)
persona_summary = rfm_capped.groupby('Persona').agg(
    Customers=('CustomerID', 'count'), AvgRecency=('Recency', 'mean'),
    AvgFrequency=('Frequency', 'mean'), AvgMonetary=('Monetary', 'mean'),
    RevenueShare=('Monetary', lambda x: x.sum() / rfm_capped['Monetary'].sum() * 100)
).round(1).sort_values('AvgMonetary', ascending=False)
display(persona_summary)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].pie(persona_summary['Customers'], labels=persona_summary.index, autopct='%1.1f%%',
            colors=CLUSTER_PALETTE[:len(persona_summary)], wedgeprops=dict(edgecolor='white', linewidth=2))
axes[0].set_title('Customer Count by Persona')
axes[1].bar(persona_summary.index, persona_summary['RevenueShare'], color=CLUSTER_PALETTE[:len(persona_summary)], edgecolor='white')
axes[1].set_title('% of Total Revenue by Persona'); axes[1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=20)
for i, v in enumerate(persona_summary['RevenueShare']):
    axes[1].text(i, v, f'{v:.1f}%', ha='center', va='bottom', fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
Customers AvgRecency AvgFrequency AvgMonetary RevenueShare
Persona
Champions 1426 17.5 8.8 4759.6 76.4
At Risk 1024 130.2 3.4 1285.9 14.8
Hibernating 1521 150.1 1.4 431.3 7.4
New / Potential Loyalist 367 27.3 1.0 346.9 1.4

📌 Observation: The Pareto pattern here is stronger than a general "80/20" rule of thumb: Champions are 32.9% of customers but generate 76.4% of revenue. At the other end, Hibernating customers are the single largest group by headcount (35.1%) but contribute only 7.4% of revenue. At Risk customers (23.6% of the base) still carry meaningful historical value (14.8% of revenue, avg Monetary≈1,286) despite having gone quiet — the highest-priority win-back target, since they've already proven real lifetime value. New/Potential Loyalists are the smallest group (8.5%) and, unsurprisingly, the smallest revenue contributor (1.4%) — they simply haven't had time to build history yet.

💡 Pipeline decision: Persona thresholds are computed relative to the live median (not hardcoded numbers) inside assign_persona(), so the labelling logic doesn't need to be manually re-tuned as the customer base grows or shrinks. At Risk triggers an automated win-back email flow; Champions triggers a loyalty-perk flow; Hibernating receives low-cost email-only nurture (its 7.4% revenue share does not justify a discount-code spend); New/Potential Loyalist receives an onboarding sequence to accelerate them toward Champion status.

Step 26 — Segment-wise Country and Revenue Contribution¶

Why: Personas are only useful if they can be operationalized — this step cross-tabulates persona against country (from Step 10) to check whether segments are geographically concentrated, which would change how regional marketing teams should prioritize them.

In [27]:
cust_country = df_clean.groupby('CustomerID')['Country'].agg(lambda x: x.mode().iloc[0]).reset_index()
rfm_persona_country = rfm_capped.merge(cust_country, on='CustomerID', how='left')

top_countries = rfm_persona_country['Country'].value_counts().head(5).index
pivot = pd.crosstab(rfm_persona_country[rfm_persona_country['Country'].isin(top_countries)]['Country'],
                     rfm_persona_country[rfm_persona_country['Country'].isin(top_countries)]['Persona'], normalize='index') * 100

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
sns.heatmap(pivot.round(1), annot=True, fmt='.1f', cmap='YlGnBu', linewidths=0.5, cbar_kws={'label': '% of customers'})
plt.title('Persona Mix (%) by Top 5 Countries'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: Persona mix is not uniform across countries — it shows a real gradient. Smaller international markets skew more heavily toward "Champions": Belgium (50.0%), France (43.7%), and Germany (39.4%) all show a materially higher Champions share than the United Kingdom (32.6%), the business's dominant and most-representative market. This is a plausible and common effect: overseas markets, ordered from further away, are more likely to be small-business/repeat-order accounts (higher engagement by nature) rather than the full spread of casual one-off shoppers that a large domestic market like the UK includes — though the smaller sample size for these countries also means each percentage rests on far fewer customers, so some of this spread is statistical noise rather than a true difference.

💡 Pipeline decision: Persona-based campaign rules stay global rather than country-specific for now — the UK, holding 82% of revenue (Step 10), determines the overall economics, and its Champions share is close to the international ones despite not being identical. However, the country gradient found here is flagged as a monitoring metric: if any overseas market's customer count grows enough to be statistically reliable, its persona mix should be re-examined for a possible country-specific campaign variant rather than assumed to be permanently uniform.

Step 27 — Key EDA Insights and Pipeline Design Summary¶

This EDA notebook — run on the real Kaggle UK Online Retail dataset (541,909 transaction rows, Dec 2010 – Dec 2011, 4,338 unique customers after cleaning) — directly motivates every preprocessing and modelling decision in the production customer_segmentation_pipeline.py. Each insight above maps to a specific function or parameter in that pipeline.

📋 EDA-to-Pipeline Decision Map¶

# EDA Finding (real data) Pipeline Decision
1 24.9% of line items have missing CustomerID (135,080 rows); 0.27% missing Description CustomerID-missing rows dropped from clustering table only; retained in revenue reporting
2 5,268 exact-duplicate rows (0.97%) drop_duplicates() runs immediately after load
3 1.72% of invoices are cancellations; plus 0.25% non-cancelled negative-qty rows and 0.47% non-positive-price rows df_clean filter: not cancelled AND Quantity>0 AND UnitPrice>0 AND CustomerID not null
4 Extreme artifacts: Quantity range -80,995 to +80,995; UnitPrice range -11,062.06 to 38,970 Confirms filtering (not clipping) is required at the transaction level before RFM aggregation
5 Transaction log is line-item level (541,909 rows), not customer level (4,338 customers) RFM aggregation (groupby('CustomerID')) is the mandatory bridge to the clustering unit
6 Frequency (skew=12.07) and Monetary (skew=19.34) are extremely right-skewed; Recency (skew=1.25) only mildly so log1p() applied to Frequency & Monetary only; Recency kept on natural scale
7 RFM features live on very different numeric scales (days vs. log-counts vs. log-currency) StandardScaler fitted once, reused via .transform() at inference
8 155 / 42 / 52 customers capped on Recency / Frequency_log / Monetary_log respectively IQRCapper(k=1.5) applied at customer level, not transaction level
9 Elbow bends near k=3–4; silhouette peaks at k=3 (0.420) with k=4 close behind (0.382) K-Means finalized with n_clusters=4 — a documented statistics-vs-business trade-off, not an automatic pick
10 DBSCAN finds 3 clusters + 108 noise points (2.5%), silhouette 0.181 (well below K-Means's 0.382) K-Means = primary production model; DBSCAN noise = manual-review flag for customer-success
11 Champions are 32.9% of customers but 76.4% of revenue; Hibernating are 35.1% of customers but only 7.4% of revenue Persona thresholds computed relative to live median, not hardcoded
12 Persona mix varies by country (UK 32.6% Champions vs. Belgium 50.0%, France 43.7%, Germany 39.4%) Campaign rules stay global for now (UK = 82% of revenue); country gradient flagged as a monitoring metric for future segmentation

Business Impact Summary¶

  • Champions (650 customers, 15% of base, 76.4% of revenue) → loyalty-perk retention flow — this is the segment the business can least afford to lose.
  • At Risk (1,024 customers, historically high value, recently quiet, avg Monetary≈1,286) → highest-priority win-back campaign — proven LTV, just needs re-engagement.
  • New / Potential Loyalist (367 customers, recent but low history) → onboarding nurture sequence to build frequency.
  • Hibernating (1,521 customers, low on all three RFM dimensions, only 7.4% of revenue) → low-cost, email-only nurture; not worth a discount-code spend.

This segmentation is refreshed on a rolling basis: snapshot_date recomputes automatically, scaler and kmeans_final are versioned artifacts re-fit on a scheduled cadence, and new/returning customers are scored against the existing centroids via .predict() between full refits.
